title: LA 3 — Test
src: Local Anesthesia — Mode of Action & Kinetics

mcqs.q: Nerve conduction depends primarily on changes within the:
mcqs.explain: Excitability and conduction relate to changes in the nerve membrane; the axoplasm/cell body mainly provide metabolic support.

mcqs.q: At rest, the interior of the nerve membrane is:
opts: Negative (−70 mV), with K⁺ inside and Na⁺ outside
Negative because Cl⁻ is actively pumped in
mcqs.explain: The resting interior is −70 mV; K⁺ stays inside and Na⁺ outside because the resting membrane is relatively impermeable to Na⁺.

mcqs.q: Depolarization of the nerve membrane is caused by:
opts: Rapid influx of Na⁺, reversing the potential to about +40 mV
Efflux of K⁺, making the inside more negative
Active pumping of Na⁺ out of the cell
mcqs.explain: Increased Na⁺ permeability lets Na⁺ rush in; the interior becomes positive (~+40 mV) — depolarization.

mcqs.q: Repolarization returns the membrane to −70 mV mainly through:
opts: Closure of all ion channels at once
mcqs.explain: After depolarization, K⁺ permeability rises and K⁺ leaves the cell, restoring the negative resting potential.

mcqs.q: The sodium-potassium pump re-establishes the resting potential by:
opts: Actively moving Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, using ATP
Moving K⁺ out and Na⁺ in without energy
mcqs.explain: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP energy to transport Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, restoring the resting gradients.

mcqs.q: The primary action of a local anaesthetic is to:
opts: Decrease the permeability of the membrane to Na⁺
mcqs.explain: LAs decrease Na⁺ permeability, setting up a 'chemical roadblock' so the impulse is neither generated nor conducted.

mcqs.q: Put the LA mechanism in correct order:
opts: Bind Na⁺-channel receptor → block channel → ↓Na⁺ conductance → threshold not reached → conduction blockade
Open Na⁺ channels → depolarise → reach threshold → conduct faster
Activate the Na⁺/K⁺ pump → hyperpolarise → conduct
Release neurotransmitter → cross synapse → excite nerve
mcqs.explain: LA binds the channel receptor, blocking Na⁺ entry; the depolarization rate falls, threshold is never reached, and conduction is blocked.

mcqs.q: According to the membrane expansion theory, the LA:
opts: Enters hydrophobic membrane regions and expands it, narrowing Na⁺ channels
Binds a specific protein receptor on the channel
Displaces calcium from the membrane surface
mcqs.explain: Membrane expansion theory: lipid-soluble LA (e.g. benzocaine) diffuses into hydrophobic regions, expands the membrane and constricts Na⁺ channels.

mcqs.q: Most local anaesthetic agents are chemically:
opts: Pure lipids with no charged group
mcqs.explain: LAs are amphipathic tertiary amines: a lipophilic and a hydrophilic end joined by an ester or amide intermediate chain.

mcqs.q: Which correctly distinguishes ester from amide local anaesthetics?
opts: Esters are hydrolysed in plasma; amides are metabolised in the liver
Esters are metabolised in the liver; amides in plasma
Both are metabolised only in the kidney
mcqs.explain: Ester LAs (e.g. procaine) are hydrolysed in plasma; amide LAs (e.g. lidocaine) resist hydrolysis and are metabolised in the liver.

mcqs.q: Currently, all clinically used injectable local anaesthetics are:
opts: A mix of esters and inorganic salts
mcqs.explain: Amides are stronger and longer-acting; all modern clinically useful injectable LAs are amides.

mcqs.q: Because base LAs are weak, poorly water-soluble and air-unstable, they are dispensed as:
opts: Hydrochloride (acid) salts dissolved in sterile water
mcqs.explain: They are treated with acid to form a salt — most commonly the hydrochloride (e.g. Lidocaine HCl) — dissolved in sterile water.

mcqs.q: Which form of the local anaesthetic crosses the lipid nerve membrane?
mcqs.explain: RN (uncharged, lipophilic) crosses the membrane; once inside, the cation RNH⁺ binds the Na⁺-channel receptor to block conduction.

mcqs.q: The form that actually binds the receptor inside the sodium channel is the:
mcqs.explain: RNH⁺ (hydrophilic cation) attaches to the receptor in the Na⁺ channel and blocks Na⁺ entry.

mcqs.q: The pKa of a local anaesthetic is the pH at which:
opts: Base (RN) and cation (RNH⁺) forms are present in equal numbers
All molecules are in the base form
All molecules are in the cation form
mcqs.explain: pKa is the pH at which base and cation forms are equal in number; clinical LAs have a pKa of about 7.5–10.

mcqs.q: A local anaesthetic with a LOWER pKa tends to have a:
opts: Faster onset (more lipophilic base at pH 7.4)
mcqs.explain: Lower pKa means more uncharged base (RN) at body pH 7.4, so more drug crosses the membrane — faster onset.

mcqs.q: Why is anaesthesia often inadequate when injected into an infected/inflamed area?
opts: The acidic pH (5–6) shifts the balance to more RNH⁺ and less RN, so less drug crosses the nerve
Infection raises the tissue pH, destroying the drug
The drug becomes too lipophilic to bind anything
mcqs.explain: Inflammation makes tissue acidic; with fewer RN base molecules, less LA crosses the membrane, reducing efficacy.

mcqs.q: The greatest anatomical barrier to diffusion of an LA solution is the:
mcqs.explain: The perineurium is described as the greatest barrier to diffusion of local anaesthetic molecules.

mcqs.q: In an inferior alveolar nerve block, the LA solution reaches the:
opts: Mantle fibres first (molars), and the core fibres last (incisors/canine)
Core fibres first, mantle fibres last
mcqs.explain: Mantle (outer) fibres are reached first and supply proximal teeth (molars); core fibres are reached last at lower concentration, so their anaesthesia is later and less profound.

mcqs.q: On recovery from the block, which fibres lose the anaesthetic effect first?
opts: All fibres at the same time
mcqs.explain: As the concentration gradient reverses, mantle fibres lose the drug first but the core fibres are the first to lose the anaesthetic effect.

mcqs.q: Increasing the protein-binding capacity of a local anaesthetic mainly increases its:
mcqs.explain: Greater protein binding gives a longer duration of action; lipid solubility governs potency and pKa governs onset.

mcqs.q: Greater lipid solubility of a local anaesthetic increases its:
mcqs.explain: The more lipid-soluble the drug, the more potent it is.

mcqs.q: For a successful nerve block, the length of nerve that should be exposed to the drug is about:
opts: Any length, as size is irrelevant
mcqs.explain: About 8–10 mm of nerve — 2–3 nodes of Ranvier — must be blocked; larger nerves are harder to block.

mcqs.q: 'Induction time' for a local anaesthetic is defined as the time from:
opts: Deposition of the solution until conduction blockade
Injection until the needle is withdrawn
Onset of recovery until full sensation returns
mcqs.explain: Induction time is the interval from deposition of the LA solution until conduction blockade is achieved.

mcqs.q: Tachyphylaxis with local anaesthetics refers to:
opts: An acute decrease in response after repeated reinjection
An allergic rash to the drug
mcqs.explain: Tachyphylaxis is an acute, short-term tolerance after repeated reinjection (shorter, weaker effect), linked to edema, lowered pH and local hemorrhage/clot.

mcqs.q: A 2% lignocaine solution contains:
mcqs.explain: 2% means 20 mg in 1 mL (and 3% = 30 mg/mL); higher concentration provides more molecules and a more potent action.

mcqs.q: Sodium bisulfite is added to LA cartridges containing epinephrine because it:
opts: Is an antioxidant that prevents epinephrine oxidation (but makes the solution more acidic)
Raises the pH to speed onset
mcqs.explain: Sodium bisulfite is an antioxidant added to stop epinephrine oxidising/browning; a side effect is a more acidic solution.

mcqs.q: The complete action potential (depolarization + repolarization) takes approximately:
mcqs.explain: The whole process needs about 1 ms — depolarization ~0.3 ms and repolarization ~0.7 ms.

mcqs.q: In the specific receptor theory, local anaesthetics act by:
opts: Binding specific receptors on the sodium channels
mcqs.explain: The specific receptor theory holds that LAs bind specific receptors on the Na⁺ channels, decreasing Na⁺ permeability and interrupting conduction.

saqs.q: Describe the ionic events of resting, depolarization and repolarization.
saqs.a: Resting — interior −70 mV, K⁺ inside, Na⁺ outside. Depolarization — Na⁺ rushes in, potential reverses to +40 mV. Repolarization — K⁺ moves out, returning to −70 mV; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (ATP) then restores the gradients.

saqs.q: Outline the mechanism of action of a local anaesthetic.
saqs.a: The LA binds the Na⁺-channel receptor → blocks the channel → ↓Na⁺ conductance → depressed depolarization → threshold not reached → no depolarization → conduction blockade.

saqs.q: Name the two accepted theories of LA action.
saqs.a: Membrane expansion theory (LA expands the membrane, narrowing Na⁺ channels — e.g. benzocaine) and the specific receptor theory (LA binds receptors on the Na⁺ channel).

saqs.q: Contrast ester and amide local anaesthetics.
saqs.a: Esters (e.g. procaine) — hydrolysed in plasma, older/topical. Amides (e.g. lidocaine) — metabolised in the liver, stronger and longer-acting; all modern injectables are amides.

saqs.q: Explain RN vs RNH⁺ and how pKa affects onset.
saqs.a: RN (uncharged base, lipophilic) crosses the nerve membrane; RNH⁺ (cation, hydrophilic) binds the Na⁺-channel receptor to block conduction. Lower pKa → faster onset (more RN base at pH 7.4); higher pKa → slower onset.

saqs.q: List the factors that influence the effect of a local anaesthetic.
saqs.a: Concentration (↑ = more potent), anatomic barrier (perineurium), pKa (↓ = faster onset), lipid solubility (↑ = more potent), and protein binding (↑ = longer duration).

saqs.q: Explain the mantle/core arrangement and define tachyphylaxis.
saqs.a: Mantle fibres (outer) supply proximal teeth (molars) and are reached first; core fibres (inner) supply incisors/canine and are reached last, less profoundly. Tachyphylaxis = an acute decrease in response after repeated reinjection (shorter, weaker effect; due to edema, low pH, hemorrhage/clot).
